answer:
Probably not merely because you’re 20 and excited about a project. Paul Graham’s default advice would be to keep learning and building while you’re in college, with an exception if your project takes off and becomes worth pursuing full time.

His reasoning is that a startup consumes your life, including the freedom to explore that makes college valuable. Success can mean committing years to one company. In 2014 he explicitly advised students against starting startups in college and said 20 wasn’t the optimal age.

As of October 2026, that hasn’t become a blanket recommendation to start immediately. He still considers running a startup incompatible with full-time study. But his emphasis has shifted toward encouraging students’ independent projects precisely because some become startups. If yours takes off, pursuing it may be reasonable, even if that means leaving college. That is an exception requiring a choice, rather than a promise that you can comfortably do both.

Assuming your project is currently exciting but hasn’t demonstrated strong demand, a practical next step is to keep developing it, put it in users’ hands, and learn what they value. Study subjects that strengthen your ability to build, and work with people you like and respect.

Reconsider full-time commitment if users keep returning, recommend it to others, or pay, and serving that demand requires more time than studying permits. Those are useful decision criteria, not a precise threshold Graham has prescribed. Before leaving, assess living costs and whether a leave of absence preserves your return option. Excitement supports building now; demand strengthens the case for committing now.
